transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Linda Kenyon.
A Pentagon official confirms the U.S. military is removing its bombers from the U.K. base targeted in a suspected terror plot.
A statement says, "We can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have been redeployed to their home stations in the United States."
The Supreme Court opens its new term tomorrow and is set to hear a landmark climate change case from the city and county of Boulder.
Colorado Public Radio's Ishaan Takour reports.
In 2018, Boulder sued the oil company's Exxon and Suncor for damages.
The suit alleges that they lied about the dangers of burning fossil fuels and should now pitch in to pay for climate-driven disasters.
Michael Girard is with the Saban Center for Climate Change Law.
They're not seeking an order that emissions be reduced or that less oil and gas and coal be mined or drilled.
They're not seeking emissions regulations. They're just seeking money damages.
The Supreme Court will not rule on the case's merits.
Instead, it's questioning whether Boulder's claims are trumped by federal law, like the Clean Air Act.
A broad ruling by the court could hamper Boulder's case and more than two dozen similar climate accountability suits nationwide.
For NPR News, I'm Ishaan Takour in Boulder.
The Trump administration is giving the public more time to comment on its proposal for unprecedented changes to the U.S. Census.
The plan would reshape the drawing of voting maps and the distribution of federal funding across the country.
NPR's Hansula Wong reports.
Public comments will now be accepted through November 2nd.
The proposal calls for excluding millions of U.S. residents from a census tally that, according to the 14th Amendment, must include the "whole number of persons" in each state.
That count is used to determine each state's share of congressional seats and electoral college votes for a decade.
The Trump administration argues the Constitution's framers did not intend for the word "persons" to include people living in the states without U.S. citizenship or a green card.
Trump officials also propose cutting questions about race and ethnicity because they see a "reduced need" for that information, which is used for civil rights enforcement.
If the proposal is finalized, it's expected to spark lawsuits, and Congress or a new presidential administration in 2029 could reverse any census changes that Trump officials make.
Hansula Wong, NPR News.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has chosen the person who will lead the investigation into two failed executions this year.
Lee called for the third-party review after last week's botched execution left Christa Pike in critical condition but alive at a local hospital.
The current lethal injection process was developed after Stanton's last review found problems with how the state inspected the drugs it uses to carry out the death penalty.
Lee says Stanton's investigation will determine if the current protocol was followed and evaluate its effectiveness from there.
In the meantime, the governor has called off the remaining executions scheduled for this year.
For NPR News, I'm Mariana Baca-Yau in Nashville.
You're listening to NPR News.
The tree that was chosen for this year's Capitol Christmas display in Washington, D.C., is being replaced because of needle-cast disease.
Lauren Patterson reports.
Officials in Idaho say the change will not delay the festivities.
The original 80-foot tall grand fir was monitored over the summer, and yellowed needles means it didn't make the cut.
The possibility that the number-one choice might have been a problem is why U.S. Forest Service officials always have a backup.
Zachary Peterson is a staff officer for the Nez Perce Clearwater National Forests.
We're on our plans to go with our backup tree, which is an Engelmann Spruce.
It's seven-six feet tall, very similar in size, very similar in shape on the Waksau power anchor blister.
The spruce will be harvested in late October.
The tree will be packaged up and sent on a whistle-stop tour throughout Idaho before its journey to Washington, D.C.
For NPR News, I'm Lauren Patterson in Kami'ai, Idaho.
Brazil is heading for a run-off between President Luis Enazio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro
after neither candidate secured more than 50 percent of the votes in order to win today's election outright.
With just over 98 percent of the vote counted, Bolsonaro came in with over 47 percent of the vote, Lula with over 44 percent of the vote.
Lula is the 80-year-old leftist incumbent president.
He is seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term.
Bolsonaro is 45 years old, a right-wing politician and close ally of President Trump.
A run-off will be October 25th.
I'm Linda Kenyon.

Supreme Court begins new term, set to hear landmark climate change case from Boulder, Colorado
Trump administration extends public comment period on controversial U.S. Census proposal through November 2nd
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee appoints investigator to review two failed executions in the state
Capitol Christmas tree in Washington, D.C. replaced due to needle-cast disease affecting grand fir
